assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a new class of quantum matter with protected edge and surface states, from a clean theoretical idea (Kane-Mele, with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) to a measured quantized edge conductance in HgTe. It sits squarely in condensed matter, links band-structure theory to spectroscopy and transport, and is a lasting field with strong electronic-structure content.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theoretical formulation of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental realization in HgTe wells. That is a natural theory-plus-experiment triad. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe prediction and the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hsieh, Hasan) are not in the credited names, so some credit is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed for over fifteen years, including ARPES and transport on many materials; the interpretation is stable and the field has matured. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee can fairly omit Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang or Hasan, who are outside the supplied names.
Overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize may be read as already recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable system, giving a new platform for strongly correlated electrons. It is a genuine surprise, much like graphene itself, and has spawned a large moire field. Theory (continuum model of the flat band) and experiment fit together.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle and flat bands; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity (with Cao et al.). MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is a defensible pair; Bistritzer's role is real but secondary, and the credited names omit Yuan Cao, who was the lead experimentalist, and also other contributors.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups worldwide, but the origin of the superconducting pairing is still debated and the field is young, so the prize would be somewhat early but not reckless.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism for superconductivity is unresolved.
Credit for Cao and others, and for earlier moire theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, is outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the workhorse for treating strongly correlated electrons and, combined with DFT (DFT+DMFT), predicts real materials spectra, the Mott transition and heavy-fermion and oxide behaviour. I know its impact in my own field and value that it ties computation to measured photoemission data. It is a method rather than a single discovery, which counts against it somewhat.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit; Georges and Kotliar built the DMFT mapping to an impurity problem. The three credited names cover the core, though Metzner is absent and Jarrell and others contributed to the numerical solvers, so the allocation is not free of dispute.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature with three decades of use and many independent implementations; quantitative reproducibility across codes is an ongoing issue but the framework is secure.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views a theoretical method as a discovery or invention.
Walter Metzner is missing from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and giant TMR in MgO tunnel junctions underlie modern magnetic read heads and MRAM. It follows naturally from the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize, combines a clear physical mechanism (spin-dependent, symmetry-filtered tunnelling, well explained by first-principles theory) with major real-world use.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin, with Yuasa and Djayaprawira, achieved the giant MgO effect in 2004, after theory by Butler and Mathon. The credited triad is reasonable, but Yuasa, Djayaprawira and the theorists Butler and Mathon are not included.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed and commercially deployed for many years; recognition is mature, perhaps even late.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize might reduce novelty.
Fair allocation among MgO experimentalists and the theory predictors is disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect gives quantized Hall conductance without an external magnetic field, from magnetism combined with topology. It is a clean, unexpected realization of a long-sought phenomenon and relevant to low-dissipation electronics and metrology. It connects magnetism and electronic structure, which I know well.
assessment.attribution: Fang, Dai and co-workers predicted QAHE in magnetically doped Bi2Te3-family materials (Yu et al. 2010); Xue's group realized it in 2013 in Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)2Te3. Haldane's 1988 model and the Chang-Moodera/Chang et al. work are conceptually central and outside the supplied names, so the attribution is contentious.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by other groups (Stanford, Würzburg), but the quantization only appears at very low temperatures and the family of materials is narrow; maturity is moderate.
uncertainties: Haldane's earlier model and its relation to the prize logic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spherical-aberration correction brought sub-angstrom resolution to electron microscopy, transforming atomic-scale imaging and spectroscopy of materials and interfaces. This is a true invention with lasting impact across materials physics, close in spirit to prized instruments. I value it for its direct link to measuring structure and spectra that theory can then explain.
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the optical design theory, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the first corrected TEM, and Krivanek in STEM is a major competitor not in the credited names. The three credited people are a coherent configuration, though the Krivanek, Dellby and Batson claim could be contested.
assessment.maturity: Widely adopted, the technology is mature and has been recognised by the Wolf and Kavli prizes. Timely and long confirmed.
uncertainties: Whether an instrumentation prize in electron optics counts as physics enough for the committee.
The STEM correction priority claim of Krivanek and colleagues is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise tunable many-body Hamiltonians, with the superfluid to Mott transition as the signature result, allowing quantitative tests of Hubbard-type models. It gives a controlled quantum simulator that bears directly on correlated-electron questions. The area is broad and its single decisive discovery is less sharp.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner, Bloch, Hansch and Esslinger demonstrated the Mott insulator and related fermionic physics. Choosing three from four credited names forces a judgment that leaves out Esslinger, and the theory-experiment balance could shift.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature and independently reproduced in many labs; quantum simulation of fermionic models has progressed but broad advantage over classical computation is still being established.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat optical lattice simulation as separate from the 2001 BEC and 2012 control prizes.
Selection among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is contentious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in the Bechgaard salts opened the field of organic superconductors and showed superconductivity next to spin-density-wave order in a low-dimensional system, an early example of unconventional pairing near magnetism. It is a clear new quantum behaviour in a material, a type of result I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Jérome's group at Orsay with Bechgaard's synthesised crystals made the 1980 discovery under pressure, a clean two-person configuration with a clear division of chemistry and physics. Other collaborators in the Orsay and Copenhagen groups contributed, but I am not certain of details; the credit appears reasonably compact.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed for over forty years with a robust body of follow-up, though the pairing symmetry is still debated; recognition would be late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Subsequent impact on technology is modest compared with other candidates.
